title: Musonius on marriage
hookLine: Musonius called marriage a full partnership of care (Musonius Rufus, Lecture 13)

cards: Who handles the dentist appointments in your house? Who remembers birthdays, notices the milk is low, sits up with the sick kid? Couples argue about it, and the question is old.
In the Roman world, marriage was usually arranged around property, heirs and family alliances, and the law gave husbands far more room than wives.
Then a Stoic teacher in Rome, the man who taught Epictetus, gave a lecture describing marriage in terms that still sound fresh.

teach.b: First, the teacher. Gaius Musonius Rufus taught Stoicism in Rome in the first century AD, and was exiled more than once by emperors who didn't like him. He wrote nothing that survives.
His lectures do, because a student wrote them down and a later anthologist, Stobaeus, kept them. Second, the lecture.

teach.h: A SHARED LIFE, CARE IN SICKNESS.
teach.b: Asked what the chief purpose of marriage is, Musonius answers: a shared life, and children. But children alone aren't enough, he says; animals have offspring too.

What makes a marriage is companionship and care for each other, in health and in sickness, at every moment, each wanting to outdo the other in caring. When that's present, he says, the marriage is beautiful.
When each looks only to their own interest, it falls apart, even under the same roof. Third, the surprising part for his time.
In other lectures, Musonius argued that women should study philosophy, because they have the same reason and the same virtues as men, and that daughters should be educated like sons.

teach.h: WHOSE GOOD ARE YOU LOOKING TO?
teach.b: He also held husbands to the same standard of faithfulness he expected of wives. He wasn't modern in everything: he still assigned men and women different work.

But the center of his picture was a partnership. Fourth, the test, partnered or not. It works for any close bond, a marriage, a friendship, a sibling: does each of you look to the other's good, or only your own?

how: Readers of Musonius Rufus often point to his Lecture 13 as an ancient description of marriage as mutual care and partnership.

o: a duty to have children and heirs
a contract joining two families' property
a partnership of shared life and mutual care

games.q: Musonius on marriage. tap the pairs.
p: the anthologist who kept his lectures
do you look to the other's good?

s: Musonius said having children alone is enough to make a marriage
he said companionship and mutual care are what make it.
Musonius argued that women should study philosophy too
they have the same reason and virtues, he said.
Musonius was modern in every way about men and women
he still assigned them different work, even as he called marriage a partnership.

games.q: a couple lives under one roof, but each looks only to their own interest. what does Musonius say about this marriage?
o: it's fine, as long as there are children.
it falls apart, even if they share a house.
games.why: Musonius says a marriage where each looks only to themselves is ruined, even under one roof. care has to go both ways.

practice: Bring to mind your closest bond, a partner, a friend, a sister, a parent, and ask Musonius's question honestly: lately, have I been looking to their good, or mostly my own? No guilt, just a look.
Then let one small, unexpected way to care for them come to mind, something from their list, not yours: the errand they dread, the call they'd love.

wordCard.voice: Koinōnia. Musonius's word for marriage: a partnership of shared life and care, each trying to outdo the other. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: partnership, sharing, communion. Musonius describes marriage as a koinōnia of life.

carryVoice: Your line: full partnership. Each one trying to outdo the other in care. See you tomorrow.
